groups.process: Guru Graphics process stage or deliverable
groups.engage: Guru Graphics engagement or sales term
groups.proof: Guru Graphics proof or compliance rule

cards.subject: Discovery phase
says: gathers what the studio must learn before any design is drawn
includes research with stakeholders and audiences
ends with a clear direction to design against
cards.use: need to understand the organisation before proposing any visual route
not: starts with the first logo sketches

cards.subject: Brand brief
says: is the written statement of goals, audience, scope and constraints for the project
gives designer and client one reference to judge the work against
cards.use: need to agree in writing what the project must achieve
not: lists the final export files delivered at the end

cards.subject: Stakeholder interview
says: asks an individual inside the client about goals, concerns and history of the brand
surfaces disagreements between leaders before design starts
cards.use: need to hear how each senior person defines success for the brand
not: measures how the public perceives the brand through a survey

cards.subject: Brand audit
says: inventories the brand assets and touchpoints the client already uses
reveals inconsistencies between how the brand appears in different places
cards.use: need to see what the current brand looks like across print, web and signage
not: compares only the visual style of competing organisations

cards.subject: Audience persona
says: describes a typical member of a target audience and what they need from the brand
keeps design decisions tied to a real reader rather than the team's taste
cards.use: are asked to justify a design choice by who it is for
not: records which colours the client likes best

cards.subject: Brand attributes
says: are a short list of adjectives that describe the personality the brand should convey
give a vocabulary for judging whether a design feels right
cards.use: need words to test whether a logo route fits the intended character
not: are the approved hex values of the palette

cards.subject: Success criteria
says: define in advance how the client will decide the work has succeeded
turn the review of concepts into a comparison against agreed measures
cards.use: hear feedback that rests only on personal preference
not: are the list of fonts allowed in the guidelines

cards.subject: Decision-maker map
says: records who can approve, who advises and who only needs informing
prevents late vetoes from people who were never consulted
cards.use: discover on the final day that a director who was never briefed must sign off
not: lists the files the studio will hand over

cards.subject: Moodboard
says: collects images, colours, textures and type samples to express a feeling
is used to agree a visual tone before detailed design
cards.use: need the client to react to a mood before any logo is drawn
not: is the final set of approved brand assets

cards.subject: Anti-moodboard
says: collects examples of what the brand should specifically not look like
exposes dislikes that clients often struggle to state directly
cards.use: find that a client keeps rejecting options without saying why
not: shows the competitors' best work to be matched

cards.subject: Brand direction
says: is the agreed route for how the identity should look and feel
narrows many possibilities into one brief for the designer
cards.use: need to choose one overall path before building the full identity
not: is the printed version of the guidelines document

cards.subject: Positioning statement
says: states for whom the brand is, what it offers and why it is different
is an internal tool that guides design, not a tagline for customers
cards.use: need one sentence that explains where the brand sits among alternatives
not: is the short phrase printed under the logo

cards.subject: Visual territory
says: is an area of visual language such as typography-led or illustration-led that a brand could occupy
lets several concepts be compared at a high level
cards.use: want to explore broad stylistic areas before refining any single logo
not: is a protected geographic region in which the logo is used

cards.subject: Concept route
says: is one fully distinct design proposal shown to the client with its rationale
differs from the other routes in idea, not just in colour
cards.use: need to present genuinely different ideas rather than variations of one
not: is a set of file exports prepared for the printer

cards.subject: Simplicity
says: keeps a logo to few elements so it is read and recalled quickly
helps a mark survive reduction and reproduction
cards.use: find a mark is cluttered with detail that vanishes when small
not: requires that a mark must use only one colour

cards.subject: Scalability
says: means the mark holds up from a favicon to a building sign
is tested by shrinking the artwork and by enlarging it
cards.use: must confirm a mark works on both a business card and a billboard
not: is achieved by saving a high-resolution JPG

cards.subject: Versatility
says: means the mark works on light and dark backgrounds and in colour and mono
calls for planned variants rather than ad hoc fixes
cards.use: need the logo to function on a coloured photo and on a white page
not: is achieved by using a different logo for each channel

cards.subject: Distinctiveness
says: makes a mark recognisable and unlike peer organisations
is checked by placing the mark beside others in the sector
cards.use: worry that a design resembles another organisation in the same field
not: is achieved by using the newest visual trend

cards.subject: Appropriateness
says: means the style suits the audience and sector rather than the designer's taste
explains why a public body and a fashion label need different marks
cards.use: are asked why a playful script is wrong for a regulator
not: demands that every logo be as simple as possible

cards.subject: Negative space
says: uses the empty area around or inside shapes to form part of the meaning
can hide a second image within the mark
cards.use: want a mark to carry a hidden second meaning in the gaps between shapes
not: is the margin that must stay free around the logo

cards.subject: Optical correction
says: adjusts shapes by eye where mathematical alignment looks wrong
lets a circle overshoot a square's edge so the two appear equal in size
cards.use: see that a triangle looks smaller than a square even though both are measured equal
not: snaps every point to a grid without exception

cards.subject: Geometric construction
says: builds a mark from circles, angles and a grid so its proportions are deliberate
helps a mark be rebuilt exactly by another designer
cards.use: need a documented way to redraw the logo from scratch accurately
not: replaces the need for any visual judgement

cards.subject: Small-size test
says: checks the mark at the smallest planned use such as a social avatar or favicon
reveals fine detail and thin strokes that disappear
cards.use: need to know if a mark is still readable at sixteen pixels square
not: checks only how the logo appears when printed on a poster

cards.subject: Black-and-white test
says: checks that the mark still works when shown in a single colour
shows if the idea depends on colour to be understood
cards.use: must prove the mark does not rely on a gradient to be understood
not: measures the legibility of the mark at tiny sizes

cards.subject: Wordmark
says: is a logo made from the organisation's name set in distinctive type
relies on letterform design rather than a symbol
cards.use: are designing a logo that is purely the name in custom lettering
not: combines a name with a separate symbol

cards.subject: Lettermark
says: is a logo built from initials
suits organisations with long names that are usually abbreviated
cards.use: must brand an organisation known by its initials
not: is a drawn picture of a real object

cards.subject: Pictorial mark
says: is a recognisable image of a real object that stands for the brand
needs the audience to connect the image to the organisation
cards.use: want a literal symbol such as a drawn bird
not: is a purely geometric shape with no real-world reference

cards.subject: Abstract mark
says: uses a non-literal geometric form that carries meaning by association
avoids tying the brand to one literal image
cards.use: want a symbol that does not depict anything specific
not: is a drawn character with a face

cards.subject: Combination mark
says: pairs a symbol and a wordmark in one logo
allows the symbol to be used alone once it is known
cards.use: need a logo where the symbol and name can also be separated
not: consists of the organisation's initials only

cards.subject: Emblem
says: encloses the name inside a badge, crest or seal shape
can be hard to reproduce at small sizes because the text sits inside the shape
cards.use: are asked for a traditional crest-style mark
not: places the symbol freely beside the name

cards.subject: Mascot
says: is an illustrated character that represents the brand
can appear in many poses and expressions
cards.use: need a friendly figure to act as the face of a brand
not: is a typographic logo made from the full name

cards.subject: Dynamic identity
says: lets the mark change within set rules while staying recognisable
depends on a strong system of constants to keep recognition
cards.use: are asked for a logo that adapts to different campaigns
not: means the logo changes at random with no rules

cards.subject: Primary palette
says: holds the main colours most associated with the brand
is used most often across materials
cards.use: need the colours that appear on most brand materials
not: holds only the colours reserved for warnings

cards.subject: Secondary palette
says: supplements the primary colours for variety and range
supports charts, illustrations and campaigns
cards.use: need extra colours for charts without overpowering the main ones
not: is the set of colours the logo must always use

cards.subject: Accent colour
says: is used sparingly to draw attention to calls to action or highlights
loses its effect when it appears everywhere
cards.use: want one colour reserved for the most important button
not: is the dominant colour of every page

cards.subject: HEX code
says: is a six-digit hexadecimal notation for an on-screen colour
is written with a leading hash symbol in web styles
cards.use: need to quote a colour in a stylesheet
not: describes ink amounts for a four-colour press

cards.subject: RGB value
says: describes a colour as red, green and blue light levels
suits screens that emit light
cards.use: are specifying a colour for a monitor or phone
not: is the specification for printing on paper with four inks

cards.subject: CMYK value
says: describes a colour as cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink amounts
suits ordinary four-colour print
cards.use: are preparing a colour for a standard printed brochure
not: is the notation used inside web stylesheets

cards.subject: Spot colour
says: is a premixed ink matched to a reference swatch book
gives a consistent result that four-colour mixing may not reach
cards.use: must reproduce an exact brand colour on a printed run with a single ink
not: is a colour that appears in only one small part of a layout

cards.subject: Gamut
says: is the range of colours a given device or process can reproduce
is why a vivid screen colour may look duller when printed
cards.use: find that a bright on-screen colour cannot be matched in print
not: is the number of colours in the brand palette

cards.subject: Contrast ratio
says: measures the difference in luminance between text and its background
is expressed as a ratio such as 4.5 to 1
cards.use: need to check if text colour on a background is readable
not: is the ratio of primary to secondary colour in a layout

cards.subject: Colour proportion
says: sets how much of each palette colour appears in a layout
stops a secondary colour from outweighing the primary one
cards.use: find campaign layouts use equal amounts of every colour and feel unfocused
not: is the minimum contrast needed for body text

cards.subject: Typeface
says: is the design of a set of letters shared across weights and sizes
is the name such as a family of letterforms
cards.use: need to name the overall design of the lettering
not: is a single digital file for one weight and style

cards.subject: Type family
says: groups related styles such as regular, italic and bold under one design
lets hierarchy be built without mixing unrelated designs
cards.use: need several weights that belong together
not: is a pair of unrelated typefaces mixed for contrast

cards.subject: Serif
says: has small finishing strokes at the ends of letter stems
is often associated with tradition and print reading
cards.use: want type with small strokes at the stem ends
not: has uniform strokes with no finishing details at the ends

cards.subject: Sans serif
says: has no finishing strokes at the ends of letter stems
is common for interfaces and signage
cards.use: want clean letterforms with no strokes at the stem ends
not: is set with small feet at the base of each stem

cards.subject: Typographic hierarchy
says: uses size, weight and spacing to show what to read first
gives headings, subheadings and body text distinct roles
cards.use: find a page where nothing stands out as the starting point
not: is a list of font licences

cards.subject: Fallback font
says: is the substitute used when the preferred font is unavailable
is chosen to resemble the brand typeface in width and proportion
cards.use: know a recipient's computer will not have the brand typeface installed
not: is the font designers use for sketches

cards.subject: Web font
says: is delivered to the browser so a site can use a custom typeface
adds load weight that should be limited to the weights actually used
cards.use: want the website to show the brand typeface on every device
not: is installed only on the designer's computer

cards.subject: Font licence
says: sets what a purchaser may do with a font, such as desktop, web or app use
is separate for each type of use and must be checked before handover
cards.use: are asked to pass fonts to the client for use on their website
not: transfers ownership of the typeface design to the buyer

cards.subject: Kerning
says: adjusts the space between a specific pair of letters
fixes awkward gaps in large type such as logos
cards.use: see an uneven gap between two particular letters in a headline
not: adjusts the spacing evenly across a whole word

cards.subject: Tracking
says: adjusts the spacing evenly across a range of letters
is often widened slightly for small capitals
cards.use: want to loosen the spacing of an entire line of capitals
not: adjusts the gap between one specific letter pair

cards.subject: Leading
says: is the vertical distance between lines of text
affects how easily the eye moves from one line to the next
cards.use: find that paragraphs look too dense because lines sit very close
not: is the horizontal gap between two letters

cards.subject: Lockup
says: is a fixed arrangement of logo elements that is always used together
keeps the relationship between symbol and name consistent
cards.use: need the symbol and name always to appear in the same arrangement
not: is a security device on printed stationery

cards.subject: Horizontal lockup
says: places the symbol and name side by side
suits wide, short spaces such as headers
cards.use: have a wide narrow space like a website header
not: places the name below the symbol

cards.subject: Stacked lockup
says: places the name below or above the symbol
suits tall or square spaces
cards.use: have a square or portrait space for the logo
not: places the name beside the symbol on one line

cards.subject: Clear space
says: is the empty margin kept around the logo
is often defined in terms of a part of the logo such as the height of a letter
cards.use: must decide how close other text may sit to the logo
not: is the smallest size at which the logo may appear

cards.subject: Minimum size
says: is the smallest dimension at which the logo stays legible
is usually given separately for print and screen
cards.use: are asked how small the logo may be printed on a pen
not: is the margin kept free around the logo

cards.subject: Secondary mark
says: is a compact version of the logo for small or square spaces
is used when the full lockup would be too small to read
cards.use: need a version that fits a social avatar
not: is a second logo for a different organisation

cards.subject: Tagline lockup
says: fixes the position and size of a strapline relative to the logo
may be separated from the logo in places where space is limited
cards.use: need to place a strapline consistently beside the logo
not: fixes the minimum print size of the logo

cards.subject: Co-brand lockup
says: sets how two organisations' logos appear together
gives each logo equal prominence unless a hierarchy is agreed
cards.use: must show the client's logo beside a partner's logo
not: places the logo on a coloured background

cards.subject: Reversed logo
says: is a light version of the logo for use on dark backgrounds
is supplied as a separate artwork file
cards.use: must place the logo on a dark photograph or navy panel
not: is a mirror image of the logo

cards.subject: Monochrome logo
says: renders the logo in a single colour
is needed for one-colour print, engraving or stamping
cards.use: must supply artwork for a single-ink print job
not: is supplied only in grey for digital use

cards.subject: Logo misuse
says: is any change to the approved logo such as stretching, recolouring or adding effects
is illustrated with don't examples in the guidelines
cards.use: see a team stretch the logo to fill a banner
not: is the use of the logo on the client's own website

cards.subject: Vector graphic
says: is defined by paths and shapes so it scales without losing sharpness
is the working format for logos
cards.use: need artwork that can be enlarged without blurring
not: is made of a fixed grid of coloured pixels

cards.subject: Raster image
says: is made of a grid of pixels at a fixed resolution
becomes blurry or blocky when enlarged beyond its size
cards.use: are handling a photograph
not: can be enlarged indefinitely without quality loss

cards.subject: SVG
says: is a vector format that browsers draw directly from text-based markup
stays sharp at any size on a web page
cards.use: want a logo on a website that stays crisp on any screen
not: is a raster format that stores a grid of pixels

cards.subject: EPS
says: is an older vector format still requested by some printers and sign-makers
has no native support for the transparency effects of newer formats
cards.use: are asked by a printer for traditional vector artwork
not: is the format a browser displays natively in an image tag

cards.subject: PDF
says: can hold vector artwork and fonts in one portable file
is a common format for sending print-ready artwork
cards.use: need to send a printer a single file that keeps fonts and layout
not: is a format for storing only raster photographs

cards.subject: AI file
says: is the native editable file of a particular vector design application
is handed over as an editable master
cards.use: need the editable original artwork from the designer's software
not: is a flat image that cannot be edited

cards.subject: PNG
says: is a raster format with lossless compression and transparency support
suits a logo placed on a coloured web background
cards.use: need a logo with a transparent background for a slide
not: is a lossy format best suited to photographs

cards.subject: JPG
says: is a raster format using lossy compression that suits photographs
has no transparency support
cards.use: need a small file size for a photograph
not: supports a transparent background

cards.subject: Outlined text
says: converts live text to shapes so the typeface is no longer needed
prevents font substitution when artwork is opened elsewhere
cards.use: must send logo artwork to a printer who lacks the font
not: makes the text editable by anyone who opens the file

cards.subject: Bleed
says: extends artwork beyond the trim edge to avoid white slivers after cutting
is commonly specified by the printer in millimetres
cards.use: are preparing a print file with colour running to the edge of the page
not: is the safe margin inside the trim where text must stay

cards.subject: Colour profile
says: describes how the numbers in a file map to real colours
must match the intended output such as screen or press
cards.use: find the same file looks different on screens and print
not: is the set of brand colour names in the guidelines

cards.subject: Favicon
says: is the small icon shown in browser tabs and bookmarks
needs to remain legible at very small pixel sizes
cards.use: need the icon that appears next to the page title in a browser tab
not: is the full colour logo displayed in the page header

cards.subject: Master artwork
says: is the single approved original from which every variant is derived
is kept in an editable vector form
cards.use: need one source file so all exports stay consistent
not: is a low-resolution preview image sent for approval

cards.subject: Brand guidelines
says: document how the identity should look, sound and be used
help people who were not in the design process apply the brand correctly
cards.use: need a reference for how staff and suppliers should use the brand
not: are a legal contract with the client

cards.subject: Brand story
says: tells where the brand comes from and why it exists
gives writers and designers a shared narrative
cards.use: need a narrative that explains the purpose behind the brand
not: lists the exact colour values

cards.subject: Do and don't page
says: shows correct and incorrect examples side by side
makes rules easier to apply than prose alone
cards.use: want to show visually how the logo must not be altered
not: lists the contact details of the studio

cards.subject: Imagery guidance
says: sets the style, subject and treatment of photographs and illustration
prevents stock images from clashing with the identity
cards.use: find that teams choose photos of very different styles
not: sets the minimum size of the logo

cards.subject: Tone of voice
says: defines how the brand sounds in writing and speech
gives example phrases that show the register
cards.use: find that emails and web pages read as if written by different organisations
not: defines the typeface for headlines

cards.subject: Accessibility standards
says: set minimum contrast and legibility requirements for brand materials
apply to colour pairings and type sizes in the system
cards.use: must ensure brand colours can be read by people with low vision
not: list the file formats of the logo

cards.subject: Guidelines version number
says: shows which edition of the rules a reader holds
lets suppliers detect that they have an outdated copy
cards.use: find suppliers working from a superseded PDF of the rules
not: sets the number of pages in the document

cards.subject: Template-led guideline
says: supplies ready-built templates alongside the rules so people apply them without interpreting
reduces drift because staff start from approved layouts
cards.use: find nobody reads a 40 page rule book but everyone uses the slide deck
not: relies on prose chapters only

cards.subject: Stationery
says: is the set of printed business items such as letterheads, envelopes and cards
carries the identity into everyday correspondence
cards.use: need to apply the identity to everyday printed correspondence
not: is a web page template

cards.subject: Email signature
says: carries a person's details at the foot of messages
needs a logo image that renders in many email clients
cards.use: find that staff set up their email sign-offs in many different styles
not: is the legal disclaimer printed on a contract

cards.subject: Presentation template
says: gives slides approved layouts, colours and type styles
reduces the chance of staff creating off-brand slides
cards.use: find every staff member builds slides from scratch in a different style
not: sets the editorial voice of the website

cards.subject: Social profile image
says: is the small cropped avatar shown on a social platform
usually needs the compact mark rather than the full lockup
cards.use: must prepare the logo for the round avatar of a social account
not: is the tiny icon shown in a browser tab

cards.subject: Signage
says: applies the identity to physical locations such as entrances and wayfinding
has to consider viewing distance, materials and lighting
cards.use: must adapt the logo for an external fascia or reception wall
not: is a digital banner on a website

cards.subject: Icon set
says: is a family of small symbols drawn with consistent stroke, corner and grid rules
extends the identity into interfaces and documents
cards.use: need a consistent set of pictograms for a website and printed material
not: is a single logo variant for small sizes

cards.subject: Print proof
says: is a sample produced before a full run to check colour and finish
catches errors that look fine on screen
cards.use: must check how a spot colour appears on the chosen paper before printing thousands
not: is a low-resolution preview emailed for review

cards.subject: Review round
says: is one cycle of the client giving feedback and the studio revising
is limited in number by the agreed scope
cards.use: need to count how many feedback cycles the agreement allows
not: is an extra route added without discussion

cards.subject: Consolidated feedback
says: combines all the client's comments into one agreed set before it reaches the designer
removes contradictions between reviewers
cards.use: receive conflicting comments from five different people
not: is feedback sent in separate emails by each reviewer

cards.subject: Named approver
says: is the one person with the authority to say the work is approved
has to be identified before the work is presented
cards.use: need a single person responsible for the final yes
not: is every member of the client's team

cards.subject: Objective-based feedback
says: judges the work against the brief and success criteria
avoids arguments that only reflect personal taste
cards.use: hear a reviewer say they simply don't like the colour
not: is feedback offered only on the logo's colour

cards.subject: Rationale
says: explains the reasoning behind a design choice in terms of the brief
moves discussion from taste to fit with the goals
cards.use: want the client to see why a route was chosen
not: is the list of changes requested by the client

cards.subject: Scope creep
says: is the gradual growth of requested work beyond what was agreed
is managed by tracking requests against the agreed scope
cards.use: find the client keeps asking for small extra pieces that were not quoted
not: is a reduction in the project's budget by the client

cards.subject: Change request
says: is a formal note that work outside the original scope is wanted
is estimated and agreed before it is carried out
cards.use: are asked mid-project to add a new application that was not in the proposal
not: is a comment on the colour of the logo

cards.subject: Revision allowance
says: is the number of revision rounds included in the agreed price
sets expectations for how many cycles of change are covered
cards.use: need to explain how many revisions the fee covers
not: is the number of concepts shown at the start

cards.subject: Sign-off
says: is the written confirmation that a stage has been approved
allows the next stage to begin without reopening the last
cards.use: need to avoid reopening earlier choices at the end
not: is the final bill for the project

cards.subject: Design by committee
says: happens when many reviewers each push for their own change
tends to produce a compromise that suits nobody
cards.use: see the logo losing its idea as each director adds a request
not: is a method for gathering structured feedback from one approver

cards.subject: Handover package
says: is the organised set of final files and documents delivered at project end
includes guidance on where each file should be used
cards.use: need to deliver everything the client needs to use the brand without the studio
not: is the first concept presentation

cards.subject: Editable working files
says: are the source files that let others edit and extend the artwork
are delivered alongside exports so future designers can continue
cards.use: want another designer to be able to adjust the artwork later
not: are flattened images sent for viewing only

cards.subject: Digital asset library
says: is an organised store of approved logos, images and templates
gives staff one trusted place to find current assets
cards.use: find staff searching old emails for the right logo file
not: is a printed manual of the guidelines

cards.subject: Copyright assignment
says: is a written transfer of rights from the creator to the client
has to be in writing to be effective in the UK
cards.use: need clarity on who owns the finished artwork
not: is the person who commissions the work automatically owning it

cards.subject: Trademark clearance
says: checks whether a name or mark conflicts with existing registrations
is a legal check that a design studio does not carry out as a legal opinion
cards.use: worry that a new mark resembles one already registered
not: confirms the logo is distinctive in its design

cards.subject: Launch plan
says: sequences the introduction of the new identity across channels
decides what changes first and what is replaced later
cards.use: must decide the order in which website, signage and stationery are changed
not: lists the brand colours

cards.subject: Rollout phasing
says: spreads the change over stages based on cost, visibility and lifetime of old material
lets low-cost digital items change at once while print runs out first
cards.use: must avoid pulping stock of old printed brochures
not: changes every item on the same day

cards.subject: Old-asset retirement
says: removes or replaces outdated logos and templates after launch
stops two versions of the brand circulating together
cards.use: find old logo files still on shared drives months after launch
not: adds new templates to the library

cards.subject: Staff toolkit
says: gives employees templates and short instructions to apply the new brand
launches the identity internally before external audiences see it
cards.use: want employees to feel ready to use the new identity from day one
not: is a press release for journalists

cards.subject: Brand governance
says: sets who owns the brand, who approves exceptions and how assets are managed
keeps the identity consistent after the studio has left
cards.use: need a process for approving requests that fall outside the guidelines
not: is the design of the logo

cards.subject: Post-launch review
says: checks after launch how the identity is being used and where it slips
produces a list of fixes and gaps in the guidelines
cards.use: want to learn what is going wrong a few weeks after launch
not: is the first discovery workshop

cards.subject: The Guru Graphics process
says: is described as From Vision to Brand
has five numbered steps from strategy to launch
cards.use: need the name of the studio's overall method
not: has three steps from concept to invoice

cards.subject: Brand Strategy step
says: comes first of the five steps
defines positioning, personality, audience, values and brand direction
cards.use: need the stage that sets the direction before any visuals
not: translates the identity into signage and stationery

cards.subject: Visual Identity step
says: is the second of the five steps
covers a distinctive logo, colour palette, typography, imagery and visual language
cards.use: need the stage where the logo, palette and type are created
not: equips teams with assets to introduce the new identity

cards.subject: Brand Guidelines step
says: is the third of the five steps
creates a clear system that keeps the brand consistent across platforms and communication
cards.use: need the stage that produces the consistency system
not: defines positioning and personality

cards.subject: Brand Applications step
says: is the fourth of the five steps
translates the identity into touchpoints from signage and stationery to digital media and presentations
cards.use: need the stage that puts the identity onto real touchpoints
not: creates the logo and colour palette

cards.subject: Brand Launch step
says: is the last of the five steps
equips teams with creative assets and direction to introduce the identity with confidence
cards.use: need the stage that prepares teams to introduce the new identity
not: defines positioning, personality and audience

cards.subject: Business Assets
says: are described by the studio as stationery, templates, presentation assets, digital icons and daily-use applications
are one of four things listed under what clients get
cards.use: need the studio's name for the everyday templates and stationery it delivers
not: are described as how the brand should look, sound and behave

cards.subject: Guidelines deliverable
says: is described by the studio as how the brand should look, sound and behave across every touchpoint
is one of four things listed under what clients get
cards.use: need the studio's description of the guidelines document
not: is described as launch assets and channel templates

cards.subject: Rollout and Launch pack
says: is described by the studio as launch assets, channel templates and handover materials
is one of four things listed under what clients get
cards.use: need the studio's name for the launch materials and handover
not: is described as stationery and presentation assets

cards.subject: Brand Discovery
says: is the first engagement and is typically three to four weeks
includes four original identity concepts and two rounds of revision on the selected route
cards.use: need the studio's shortest engagement
not: is the engagement that includes 30 to 60 page guidelines

cards.subject: Identity Programme
says: is the second engagement and is typically six to eight weeks
adds complete stationery, templates, a digital asset library and editable working files to Brand Discovery
cards.use: need the engagement that adds stationery and templates
not: is the engagement scoped per organisation with no typical duration

cards.subject: Brand System
says: is the third engagement and is typically eight to twelve weeks
adds 30 to 60 page guidelines, brand voice, campaign style and accessibility and contrast standards
cards.use: need the engagement that includes full brand guidelines and voice
not: is the engagement that includes a launch kit for every owned channel

cards.subject: Rollout Programme
says: is the fourth engagement and is scoped per organisation
adds a launch kit, estate and signage rollout plan, staff toolkit, governance and a post-launch support window
cards.use: need the engagement that covers the rollout across an organisation's estate
not: is the engagement typically complete in three to four weeks

cards.subject: Request a proposal
says: is the call to action on each engagement
reflects that engagements are scoped and quoted against the client's requirements
cards.use: need the button text on the engagement cards
not: is the closing call to action at the end of the page

cards.subject: Start a Conversation
says: is the closing call to action
invites the client to say where the organisation is today and where the brand should go
cards.use: need the studio's closing invitation
not: is the button on each engagement card

cards.subject: Procurement ready
says: is one of the studio's three headline strengths
reflects that enterprise and public sector buyers work through proposals and procurement
cards.use: need to explain why the studio sells by proposal rather than fixed packages
not: means the studio publishes fixed prices with a Book Now button

cards.subject: Your Reputation Engine
says: is the public sector section heading that replaces the word growth
is built on trust, recognition, standing apart from peers and engagement and loyalty
cards.use: need the framing the studio uses for public sector buyers
not: is the heading used for private sector growth messaging

cards.subject: Design-only scope
says: means the studio does design and branding only
excludes software, development, hosting and support
cards.use: are asked whether the studio can host a client's website
not: means the studio also sells development and support

cards.subject: Who Trusted Us wall
says: shows logos of organisations the studio has delivered design or branding work for
presents each logo as a record of work, not an endorsement
cards.use: are asked what the client logos on the home page mean
not: shows organisations that have endorsed the studio

cards.subject: Written permission for client marks
says: is needed before showing a client's logo because large organisations restrict who may display it
is a rule in the studio's own notes for each mark it shows
cards.use: are about to add a new client logo to the clients wall
not: is unnecessary because the studio designed the work

cards.subject: Testimonials
says: are reproduced exactly as the clients wrote them
must not be edited because doing so is dishonest and, under the DMCC Act 2024, a regulatory problem
cards.use: are tempted to tidy the wording of a client quote
not: may be shortened and reworded for style

cards.subject: Credentials page
says: renders a row only when it is filled in and shows on request for the rest
must not publish cover levels or certifications the studio does not hold
cards.use: need to complete the supplier details procurement teams look for
not: lists insurance cover levels before they are verified

cards.subject: Enquiry form consent
says: requires the form to say what the address is used for and link the policy
backs the newsletter promise that the address is used for the newsletter only
cards.use: are asked what the enquiry form must tell people
not: lets the address be used for any marketing

cards.subject: Registered company details
says: must show the registered name, number, place of registration and registered office on a UK limited company's website
appear in the footer on every page of the studio's site
cards.use: need to know where the company's registration details are shown
not: appear only on the credentials page

qa.q: Which file type should you give a web developer so the logo stays sharp at any size on a page?
qa.right: SVG
wrong: A scanned print of the logo
qa.why: SVG is a vector format, so it scales without blurring and browsers draw it directly.

qa.q: What is a brand brief?
qa.right: A written statement of goals, audience, scope and constraints that the work is judged against
wrong: The final set of approved logo files
A contract that fixes the invoice dates
qa.why: It is the shared reference for the project.

qa.q: A client wants a logo made only from their name set in distinctive lettering. What type of mark is this?
qa.right: A wordmark
qa.why: A wordmark is built from the full name; a lettermark uses initials.

qa.q: Which colour notation is normally used in a website stylesheet?
qa.right: HEX or RGB
qa.why: Screens use light, so web styles use HEX, RGB and similar notations.

qa.q: Which colour model should the printer receive for a standard four-colour brochure?
qa.right: CMYK
qa.why: Four-colour presses mix cyan, magenta, yellow and black inks.

qa.q: What does a brand guidelines document do?
qa.right: Explains how the identity should look, sound and be used so others can apply it correctly
wrong: Replaces the need for any logo files
qa.why: Its job is consistent application by people who were not in the design process.

qa.q: A reviewer says: 'I just don't like the blue.' What is the best first response from the designer?
qa.right: Ask how the blue relates to the brief and success criteria, and what it should convey instead
wrong: Change the blue immediately to avoid a delay
Tell the reviewer their taste is wrong
Ignore the comment until the final round
qa.why: Moving the discussion to the brief turns taste into something that can be assessed.

qa.q: A printer asks for artwork with a 3 mm bleed. What does this mean?
qa.right: Extend background colour or images 3 mm beyond the trim edge
wrong: Keep all text 3 mm inside the trim edge
qa.why: Bleed prevents white slivers when pages are cut slightly off.

qa.q: A logo looks fine on a laptop but its thin strokes disappear on a business card. What should be done?
qa.right: Simplify or thicken the details and set a minimum size for the mark
wrong: Print the card at a higher resolution only
qa.why: The problem is the design's scalability; a minimum size rule and simpler detail address it.

qa.q: A team stretches the logo to fill a wide banner. What is this called in guidelines?
qa.right: Logo misuse
qa.why: Stretching distorts the approved proportions and appears in the don't examples.

qa.q: Which statement best describes clear space?
qa.right: The empty margin kept around the logo where no other elements may sit
wrong: The smallest size the logo may be printed
The gap between letters inside the logo
The background colour behind the logo
qa.why: Clear space protects the logo from crowding; minimum size is a separate rule.

qa.q: Which format supports transparency and uses lossless compression?
qa.right: PNG
qa.why: PNG has an alpha channel and lossless compression; JPG is lossy and has no transparency.

qa.q: Which pair makes up a combination mark?
qa.right: A symbol and a wordmark
wrong: A crest and a slogan only
qa.why: A combination mark pairs a symbol with the name.

qa.q: A client gives feedback from five staff members in five separate emails with conflicting requests. What should the studio ask for?
qa.right: One consolidated set of feedback from the named approver
wrong: To apply all of them and see what works
To apply the first email only
qa.why: Consolidation removes contradictions before the designer works.

qa.q: You are asked to check this CSS for brand safety. What is the problem for users whose browser lacks the brand font?
qa.right:
font-family: 'BrandSerif Display';
font-size: 18px;
qa.wrong: There is no fallback font, so the browser will choose an unsuitable default
why: The font-size should be written in hex
The family name must be written in uppercase
Quotes are not allowed around font names
qa.code: A stack should end with a fallback such as a generic serif family that resembles the brand font.

qa.q: Which CSS defines the brand palette so it can be reused across a stylesheet?
qa.right: Custom properties such as --brand-primary: #0a3d62; on :root
wrong: A separate image for every colour
Inline colours typed in each element
A comment with the hex values
qa.why: Custom properties keep a single source of truth that guidelines can reference.

qa.q: What does this markup provide for a website's brand?
qa.right: The small icon shown in browser tabs
wrong: The logo in the page header
qa.why: A rel=icon link supplies the favicon.

qa.q: Which minimum contrast ratio does the common AA level ask for normal-size body text?
qa.why: AA needs 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text; 7:1 is the AAA level.

qa.q: A palette needs an accent for the main button, but the designer is tempted to use it for headings, icons and borders as well. What is the risk?
qa.right: The accent loses its power to draw attention
wrong: The palette will print in RGB
The contrast ratio of the whole palette changes
qa.why: An accent works because it is used sparingly.

qa.q: A client asks for a logo that includes their full name inside a badge shape. What is a drawback of an emblem for small uses?
qa.right: Text inside the badge becomes illegible at small sizes
qa.why: Fine text inside a shape is hard to read when reduced.

qa.q: What is the difference between kerning and tracking?
qa.right: Kerning adjusts one pair of letters; tracking adjusts the spacing across a range of letters
wrong: Kerning changes line spacing; tracking changes letter height
Kerning is for print only and tracking for web only
qa.why: Leading is the line spacing.

qa.q: A designer sends a logo file to a printer who lacks the brand font and the text shows in a different font. What was missed?
qa.right: Converting the text to outlines before sending
qa.why: Outlined text no longer depends on installed fonts.

qa.q: Why is the font licence checked before handover?
qa.right: Desktop, web and app use are licensed separately and the client may need rights the studio did not buy
wrong: The licence transfers copyright of the design
Fonts cannot be shared in any case
The licence sets the size of the logo
qa.why: Licences cover specific uses; the client must hold the ones they need.

qa.q: Which version of the logo should be used on a dark navy panel?
qa.right: The reversed (light) version
qa.why: A reversed logo is made for dark backgrounds.

qa.q: Which test best shows a logo does not depend on colour to be understood?
qa.right: Rendering it in one colour on white and on black
qa.why: The black-and-white test strips colour from the idea.

qa.q: A pitch shows three routes that are the same logo in three colours. What is wrong?
qa.right: They are variations, not genuinely different concept routes
wrong: Three routes is too few for any project
Colour is never part of a logo
The routes should have used the same font
qa.why: Concept routes should differ in idea.

qa.q: Which is the best reason to include an anti-moodboard?
qa.right: It reveals dislikes the client cannot easily state
wrong: It proves the client was wrong
qa.why: Seeing what to avoid clarifies direction.

qa.q: A request for a new application not in the proposal arrives mid-project. What is the right step?
qa.right: Treat it as a change request, estimate it and agree it before doing it
wrong: Do it quietly to keep goodwill
Include it in the next review round free of charge
qa.why: Tracking work against the agreed scope controls scope creep.

qa.q: A client wants to know who owns the final artwork. What do you say in the UK?
qa.right: Rights need to be assigned in writing; commissioning alone does not automatically transfer them
wrong: The client owns everything automatically on payment
qa.why: Under UK law the creator is first owner unless there is a written assignment or another rule applies; the studio should take legal advice for specifics.

qa.q: A page of rules with correct and incorrect examples side by side is best described as what?
qa.right: A do and don't page
qa.why: Visual examples make the rule easier to apply.

qa.q: Which is true of the Guru Graphics Brand Discovery engagement, according to the studio's own description?
qa.right: It typically takes three to four weeks and includes four original identity concepts and two rounds of revision
wrong: It is scoped without any typical duration
It includes a launch kit for every owned channel
qa.why: The durations are typical, not promises.

qa.q: According to the studio, what does the Brand System engagement add to the Identity Programme?
qa.right: 30 to 60 page guidelines, brand voice and accessibility and contrast standards
wrong: A launch kit for every owned channel
qa.why: Each engagement includes everything in the one before and adds its own items.

qa.q: A reviewer asks the studio to edit a client testimonial for style before publishing. What should the studio do?
qa.right: Publish it exactly as written or not at all
wrong: Reword it to match the house voice
qa.why: The studio's rule is that testimonials stay exactly as the clients wrote them.

qa.q: A mark is a circle beside a square of the same measured height. The circle looks smaller. What should the designer do?
qa.right: Let the circle overshoot slightly using optical correction
wrong: Reduce the circle by exactly the same amount
Change both to the same hex colour
qa.why: Round shapes need to overshoot to look equal in size.

qa.q: A client sees colour look different on screen and in print for the same file. What is the most likely cause?
qa.right: Different gamuts and colour profiles for screen and press
wrong: The file is in the wrong language
The logo has too much clear space
qa.why: Screens and presses reproduce different ranges of colour.

qa.q: The final day of the project reveals a director who was never briefed must sign off, and she dislikes the route. What would have prevented this?
qa.right: A decision-maker map built during discovery
qa.why: Mapping approvers early avoids late vetoes.

qa.q: A brand launch replaces everything on one day, including 20,000 leaflets still in stock. What is the better approach?
qa.right: Phase the rollout, changing digital items at once and printed items as stock runs out
wrong: Pulp the leaflets to keep the launch clean
Delay the whole launch for a year
qa.why: Rollout phasing balances cost and visibility.

qa.q: A team finds three different versions of the logo in circulation six months after launch. What practice should have addressed this?
qa.right: Brand governance with a single digital asset library and retirement of old assets
qa.why: Governance keeps one current set of assets and retires the old.

qa.q: A guidelines document is 60 pages and staff ignore it. What is a sensible fix?
qa.right: Provide ready-made templates and a short quick-start alongside the document
qa.why: Templates let people apply the brand without interpreting rules.

qa.q: A large charity partner wants its logo beside the client's. What should the studio define?
qa.right: A co-brand lockup with rules for relative size and spacing
wrong: Nothing, because logos never appear together
A new combined logo for both
qa.why: Co-branding rules prevent one logo overwhelming the other.

qa.q: A designer exports an icon set with different stroke weights and corner radii for each icon. What principle did they miss?
qa.right: Consistent construction rules across the set
qa.why: An icon family needs shared stroke, corner and grid rules.

qa.q: A client asks you to confirm a new name is free to register as a trademark. How should the studio respond?
qa.right: Explain that a design check is not a legal clearance and recommend a qualified professional
wrong: Say the name is fine because the logo is unique
Register it for them without advice
Say trademarks do not apply to names
qa.why: Clearance is a legal check, not a design opinion.

qa.q: A web developer receives a 4 MB PNG logo to put in the header. Which is a better choice?
qa.right: A properly exported SVG, with a PNG fallback only if needed
qa.why: SVG is small and sharp at any size.

qa.q: The client's secondary colour is used in equal quantity to the primary in every layout and the brand feels unfocused. What is the fix?
qa.right: Define colour proportions so the primary leads and the secondary supports
qa.why: Proportion rules give the palette a clear order.

qa.q: The client demands the logo fit a 16 by 16 pixel favicon with all its detail. What is the best response?
qa.right: Create a simplified secondary mark for tiny sizes and keep the full lockup for larger uses
wrong: Shrink the full logo and accept the blur
Remove the logo from the site
qa.why: Small sizes need a purpose-made compact mark.

qa.q: A public sector client is asked for proof of cover and certifications by a procurement team. What is the studio's stated approach to such details on its own credentials page?
qa.right: Show a row only when it is filled in with a real, verified value, and show on request for the rest
wrong: Publish the expected values until confirmed
qa.why: Publishing a cover level or certification you do not hold is the mistake procurement teams never forgive.

qa.q: Which statement about a dynamic identity is accurate?
qa.right: It stays recognisable because a set of constants stays fixed while other elements vary within rules
qa.why: The constants carry recognition.

qa.q: Two reviewers want opposite changes, and the named approver is unavailable for two weeks. What is the best action?
qa.right: Record the conflict, agree a decision date with the client and pause the affected work
qa.why: Without an approver, the project needs an explicit decision path to avoid wasted rounds.

qa.q: A client wants the logo changed to a darker blue to meet contrast needs on white, but the brand palette already has a darker tone. What is the better route?
qa.right: Use the darker tone for text and keep the logo colour, documented in the accessibility rules
qa.why: Accessibility rules can assign colours to uses without altering the logo.

qa.q: A client's logo uses a gradient that cannot be reproduced on an engraved award. What is the best planned answer?
qa.right: A monochrome version defined in the guidelines for engraving and stamping
qa.why: Planned variants avoid ad hoc fixes.

qa.q: A client asks for a guidelines PDF only, with no editable files, to avoid reworking costs. What is a risk?
qa.right: Future designers cannot extend or fix the artwork without rebuilding it
wrong: The PDF will have no colours
qa.why: Editable working files allow continued use of the artwork.
